headline: In yoron, 世 is a daiyōji replacing 輿.
ベッド is borrowed from English bed.
バー is borrowed from English bar, and is a doublet of バール and バル.
Tasuke is the continuative stem of the verb 助ける (tasukeru, “to help, to aid, to assist”).
Kango is from Middle Chinese 漢語, “Han, Chinese + speech, language”.
Ōzora is 大 (ō-, “large”) plus 空 (sora, “sky”).
Sozai is 素 (so, “element”) plus 材 (zai, “material”).
ジーパン is a blend of ジーンズ (jīnzu, “jeans”) and パンツ (pantsu, “pants”).
Hisoka goes back to Old Japanese and Proto-Japonic.
Tsūsetsu is 痛 (tsū, “severe”) plus 切 (setsu, “keen”).
フリー is borrowed from English free.
Miki was originally a compound of 身 (mi, “body”) plus 木 (ki, “tree”), first cited to a text from 1726.
In haki, 棄 is a daiyōji replacing 毀.
ボイコット is borrowed from English boycott.
Shuhō is from the Middle Chinese compound 手法, which modern Mandarin shares.
Sukuu, “to scoop”, is cognate with 救う (sukuu, “to save”).
ノー is borrowed from English no.
Bōtō is uncertain, but may be from written Chinese 冒頭 (màotóu), 冒 (“to emerge”) plus 頭 (“the head; the top; the beginning”).
パターン is borrowed from English pattern.
ガレージ is borrowed from English garage, perhaps from British English, and from French garage.
タイマー is from English timer.
Wabi is the continuative stem of the verb 詫びる (wabiru, “to apologise”).
To, “metropolitan”, is from Middle Chinese 都 (MC tu).
グループ is borrowed from English group.
Hōjiru is a shift from the verb 報ずる (hōzuru), as -uru verbs moved to the -iru pattern.
キャッチ is borrowed from English catch.
Tentai is from Middle Chinese 天體, analysable as 天 (ten, “heaven”) plus 体 (tai, “body”).
Ren'ai is from Middle Chinese 戀愛.
ブザー is from the spelling pronunciation of English buzzer.
カメラマン is borrowed from English cameraman.
